..
As of 206 AM Monday...

KEY MESSAGE 1... There is a chance for showers and thunderstorms 
this afternoon to early evening along and east of the I-95 corridor.

Satellite imagery and surface observations indicate a weak 
surface low developing over central SC, with a stalled cold 
front extending from the NC Coastal Plain into central SC. 
Dynamic guidance indicates the surface low will track east- 
northeast today into the Sandhills and central/southern Coastal 
Plain. As it does, the stalled front is expected to buckle 
westward, potentially reaching as far west as the Wake/Johnston 
county line. 

A sharp moisture gradient remains across the state: the 00z MHX 
sounding highlighted a very moist airmass over eastern NC, 
contrasted with much drier air at GSO (PWAT of ~0.85 inches). 
Surface dewpoints in the mid-70s along the coast underscore the high 
moisture content east of the boundary. An enhanced seabreeze 
interaction with the front and surface low will serve as the primary 
trigger for convective initiation, with resultant outflows likely 
driving secondary cell development.

Spatial Focus & Model Guidance: The highest storm coverage is 
expected along and east of I-95, extending from the eastern 
Sandhills into the Coastal Plain. Most CAMs keep convective activity 
concentrated over the southern Coastal Plain (primarily Sampson
and Wayne Counties). However, the RRFS represents a reasonable 
worst-case scenario, bringing convection as far west as the 
Harnett/Cumberland county line. While model spread leaves some 
uncertainty regarding exact western extent, the thermodynamic 
environment along and east of I-95 will easily support severe 
storms, characterized by MLCAPE of 2000-3000 J/kg (highest in 
Sampson County) and 30 kts of deep-layer shear. Should storms 
initiate further north near RWI, effective shear could reach ~40
kts under the influence of an upper-level jet streak.

Hazards: SPC expanded the Marginal Risk for severe thunderstorms, 
focused mainly over Sampson and Wayne Counties. The primary 
hazard will be locally damaging wind gusts, although a secondary
hail threat is also possible given straight hodographs. SPC has
also maintained a 2-percent tornado risk, where a Slight Risk 
of severe now exists over far southern Sampson; given weak bulk 
low-level shear, any brief tornado threat would be strictly non-
supercellular, tied to localized low-level vorticity stretching
along the surface low/boundary. Should 12z guidance and AI 
model trends continue shifting westward, further expansion of 
the severe risk westward may become necessary.

Drier, more comfortable conditions are expected Tuesday as high
pressure builds in from the north. Lower dewpoints will 
maintain comfortable humidity levels across central NC. Isolated
storm development will be largely suppressed, restricted to the
sea breeze over Sampson or Cumberland counties. The aggressive 
HRRR solution was discounted in favor of global model consensus,
which depicts a sufficiently stable airmass to prevent 
widespread activity.


KEY MESSAGE 2... Diurnally maximized convection returns to 
central NC as early as Wednesday, but more likely Thursday into 
Friday before shifting towards the coast through the weekend.

A closed mid/upper level low over southern Quebec Tues morning will 
continue to slowly pivot east-northeast as another series of 
shortwaves parade across Great Lakes and southern Ontario through 
Fri. Moisture returns in the low lvls as early as Wed, with deeper 
moisture return on Thurs, although rich tropical moisture appears 
limited in duration as the mid/upper level flow turns west-northwest 
again over the Mid-Atlantic into the Carolinas by this weekend. 
Nevertheless, this should support diurnally driven convection as 
surface dew points in the 70s return and PWAT values rise back to 
around or slightly-above normal into the weekend. There may be some 
mixing out of dew points each afternoon, especially over the 
Piedmont back into the 60s which may limit the moderate instability 
to the Sandhills and Coastal Plain.

Thurs still appears to have the best chance for measurable 
precipitation with neutral H5 height tendencies and potential 
influence from any MCV's from upstream convection over the Ohio and 
Tennessee Valley's. Reasonable high-end totals for any given area 
will be around 1" to as much as +2" based on the 12z LREF. However, 
these amounts will not occur everywhere, as is the nature of 
summertime convection, with most locations likely to receive 
somewhere between trace amounts to 0.5". Slow evolving longwave 
troughing to the west will favor southwesterly moisture transport 
over the area as early as Wed and continuing into Thurs night. This 
pattern could be conditionally favorable for excessive rainfall 
anywhere but highly dependent on training storms to develop.
